The Way of the World. William Congreve's brilliant Restoration comedy of wit, intrigue, and marriage negotiation, set among the fashionable society of London, centring on the courtship of Mirabell and Millamant.

Mirabell, a wealthy rake, loves Millamant, a rich widow with her own fortune and fierce independence. Both insist on marriage contracted between equals rather than mastery. Yet standing in their way is Lady Wishfort, Millamant's formidable aunt and guardian of her wealth, who despises Mirabell and prefers the foppish Sir Wilfull Witwoud as a suitor.

Mirabell employs a servant named Waitwell to woo Lady Wishfort under a false identity, extracting leverage through her vanity. This subplot of servant intrigue parallels the main romance.

The play contains a famous scene where Mirabell and Millamant negotiate the actual terms of their union. Each stipulates conditions. She retains her social freedom and independence. He accepts her terms. Their mock-legal exchange becomes a form of courtship and combat rolled into one.

Fainall, Mirabell's rival, is married to the deceitful Mrs. Fainall and schemes to control Millamant's fortune. But his plot unravels when his own infidelities are exposed. Through combined wit, honesty between themselves, and the exposure of their rivals' hypocrisy, Mirabell and Millamant triumph.

The play's language dazzles with puns and epigrams. Dialogue itself becomes a form of warfare. Victory belongs to the quickest wit. Millamant stands as arguably the first truly autonomous female comic protagonist, witty and wealthy and insistent on her own terms. Congreve brought Restoration comedy to its apex, perfecting its emphasis on wit, sexual intrigue, and verbal virtuosity.
